header: Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Emily Cho (Redwood SE), Mike Reynolds (OpenEnterprise CTO), Priya Das (Head of ML), Daniel Wu (Infra Lead), Aisha Gomez (Security)
summary: Deep technical session on long-context (128k+) performance: streaming latency, throughput, KV cache strategies, batching, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps to run benchmarks, share network checklist, and scope pilot for Dedicated environment.
topics: sharded KV cache and prefix caching strategies
VPC/on-prem deployment constraints, KMS/HSM, air-gapped setups
transcript: [00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Alright, thanks everyone for joining. We're gonna run through the 128k long context perf deep-dive. timebox about 50 minutes, cover benchmarks, caching, batching, on-prem constraints, and then next steps.

[00:18] Mike (OpenEnterprise): Yep, thanks Jordan. Quick note on our side: our primary goal is consistent under-150ms token tail latency for interactive querying over 100k docs, and we also have batch analytics jobs that need max throughput. We want to see if the Dedicated option can hit both cost + latency targets.

[00:35] Samira (Redwood SE): Great, that's helpful. A couple clarifying q's before we dive in — what's your current model family and quantization? And are you planning streaming for the user-facing app or precompute embeddings?

[00:50] Priya (OpenEnterprise): We're evaluating Llama-3-70B family variants and a custom finetune for summarization. Currently running int8 on-prem experiments but quality hit's a bit variable. Mostly streaming for interactive search, some background batch summarization.

[01:10] Daniel (OpenEnterprise Infra): On infra, we have a VPC in AWS us-west-2, corp firewall rules are strict; on-prem air-gapped is a possibility for PHI workflows. We use HashiCorp Vault + AWS KMS for secrets. Latency to our users needs to be low in NA and EU.

[01:30] Emily (Redwood): Thanks. We'll cover both Hosted and Dedicated topologies — for the 128k context you likely need model variants with attention optimizations and sharded KV; Dedicated gives you more predictable throughput and lets us tune kernel selection and batching windows.
[02:02] Speaker 1: Quick note, sometimes the verbal transcription messes up Redwood names, sorry if the auto transcript is odd here.

[02:20] Samira (Redwood SE): Ok jumping into architecture: for 128k+ we recommend a hybrid of prefix/KV caching plus chunking strategies. The idea is to keep the hot prefix and windowed KV shards in memory so generation avoids re-decoding long prefixes every request. We also use continuous batching to amortize kernel launch costs.
[02:48] Priya (OpenEnterprise): When you say "sharded KV", can you clarify — do you mean split KV across GPUs or across disk-backed shards? Concern is memory footprint on a single node.

[03:05] Samira: Good q — both. For Dedicated we typically shard KV across GPUs (horizontal sharding) so each GPU holds a subset of the KV space for recent tokens; for colder data we maintain a disk-backed LRU that can be prefetched. That reduces peak GPU memory but adds complexity around prefetch latency.
[03:32] Daniel: Prefetching sounds risky for tail latency. How do you avoid stalls when you miss in the in-memory shard?

[03:45] Samira: We do two things: 1) predictive prefetch based on access patterns (e.g., conversational prefixes), and 2) fallbacks to a lower-cost model variant in the same cluster for quick responses while we bring the full context in. Also micro-batching helps hide prefetches within the token pipeline.
[04:10] Mike: Ok — what's realistic streaming tail latency for 1-2 token steps with a 128k seed using your Atlas/Redwood runtime?

[04:25] Samira: On Atlas 8xA100-like infra, with optimized kernels and sharded KV, we're seeing median per-token tail latencies in the 80-160ms range for 70B-class models at 128k with continuous batching tuned. Worst-case tails can be higher on cold-cache misses. That's why we talk about SLA + fallback policies.
[04:50] Priya: Those numbers sound promising. How much does quantization to Q4 or Q5 affect that latency vs int8, and what's the quality tradeoff?

[05:05] Emily: Quantization mainly helps memory footprint and slightly reduces kernel compute time. Q4_0 / Q5 gives big memory wins enabling more KV in GPU memory — that directly reduces cache-miss latency. Int8 (the hardware INT8 path) can be faster for some kernels but quality sometimes drops more than Q4. We recommend A/B evals on your finetune set; we'll include quality delta numbers in the benchmark csv.
[05:34] Daniel: Can you share example numbers? e.g., Q4 vs INT8 on perplexity or ROUGE for summarization?

[05:45] Samira: We'll run it on your sample dataset, but ballpark — Q4 often has <2-3% quality degradation vs FP16 on many workloads, INT8 can be higher and more model-dependent. The huge win is memory which allows more KV in RAM, often improving effective end-user latency.
[06:05] Mike: Let's talk chunking — we have docs up to 1M tokens. How do you recommend chunking for retrieval + generation?

[06:18] Samira: Strategy we use: 1) Retrieval step that picks relevant spans of source docs; 2) stream those spans into a prefix with semantic chunking boundaries; 3) keep a rolling KV window for immediate context and offload older tokens to a disk LRU indexed by position. For 1M token sources you want to maintain an index so you only materialize the top-k spans per query, not the entire doc.
[06:45] Priya: When you stream many chunks in, do you re-embed or reuse embeddings?

[06:52] Emily: Reuse mostly. Embed once and cache embeddings in Redis-like store; retrieval is vector-similarity. The trick is mapping embeddings to token positions so when you assemble prefix you can fetch the exact token spans and prefetch necessary KV shards.
[07:10] Daniel: On networking — our VPC has egress restrictions and proxy for HSM calls. How does private deployment handle KMS/HSM calls?

[07:22] Emily: For Private deployments we integrate with your KMS/HSM via IAM endpoints or HC Vault transit. We're flexible: can use AWS KMS direct, CloudHSM, or on-prem appliances. For air-gapped we support customer-managed HSM with an offline key unwrap flow; that does increase initial setup time but works for PHI compliance.
[07:45] Aisha (Security): What about audit logs and tamper-proofing?

[07:50] Samira: We produce per-call audit logs with SHA-256 hashes, and we can forward logs to your SIEM. For Dedicated/Private we can stream to your S3/GCS or push via syslog. We also support immutable append-only storage for critical audit trails.
[08:12] Mike: Back to perf — batching windows: how do you pick batch window size vs SLOs?

[08:25] Samira: It's a tradeoff. Larger windows give better throughput but increase median latency. We tune based on your traffic pattern: interactive flows use tight windows (20-50ms) plus continuous batching that accumulates between token generation steps; background jobs can use larger windows. For example, we saw a 2-3x throughput gain moving window from 20ms to 80ms on certain workloads.
[08:52] Priya: Any guidance on GPU type? We have access to A100 and H100 nodes.

[08:59] Samira: H100 has better sparsity & tensor-core perf for some kernels so it's lower latency on FP16 and INT8 kernels, but A100 is a solid predictable choice. For 128k, memory matters a lot — more memory per GPU reduces KV shard misses. So pick the largest memory instance you can, or use sharding across more GPUs.
[09:20] Daniel: Does Redwood runtime support offloading parts of KV to host CPU to reduce GPU memory pressure?

[09:26] Samira: Yes — host-side KV paging is supported; we treat it as a tiered cache: GPU RAM -> Host RAM -> NVMe. We optimize placement based on access heatmaps so the most frequently accessed KV stays on GPU.
[09:40] Mike: Alright, could you walk through a concrete request path for a streaming query with a 120k prefix?

[09:48] Samira: Sure — step 1: retrieval identifies ~4-8 relevant spans, we materialize and chunk them into the prompt. Step 2: prefix builder consults KV index and determines which shards are needed; it requests prefetches to GPU. Step 3: while prefetch happens, the first tokens stream back using cached context, continuous batching collects other requests, then the runtime emits next-token predictions and appends new KV entries to the shard. If a shard miss occurs we can either do on-the-fly fetch from NVMe or fall back to a smaller model variant to maintain latency.
[10:28] Priya: You mentioned fallbacks. How transparent is switching models mid-request? Any consistency issues?

[10:34] Samira: (laughs) sorry typo — switching is controlled via policy. We don't splice outputs between models; we run the request on the fallback variant from start if we detect a likely miss. It's a policy decision tradeoff: degrade quality for latency vs block until full context is available.
[10:50] Daniel: For our compliance use-case, we can't send raw data to hosted environments. Private deployment is required for some tenants. How different is the feature set in Private vs Dedicated?

[11:05] Emily: Feature parity is high for core runtime, but hosted analytics/console integrations are optional in Private. Dedicated is managed by Redwood but isolated; Private gives you control over network and KMS. Some advanced observability metrics might require extra connectors but we can enable them.
[11:28] Aisha: On encryption at rest, do you support envelope encryption with customer-managed keys?
[11:33] Emily: Yes — we support envelope encryption and customer-managed KMS. For Dedicated we can bring-your-own-key (BYOK) and rotate keys via Vault/HSM.
[11:45] Mike: Ok, sample benchmarks — can you show plots?

[11:50] Samira: I'll summarize verbally and we'll attach the sheet after: on our Atlas 8xA100 cluster, 70B model, 128k seed, continuous batching tuned, median streaming token latency ~95ms, p95 ~320ms; with Q4 and more KV in memory median drops to ~80ms and p95 to ~210ms. Cold-cache miss p99 can go into seconds if we fetch from NVMe.
[12:20] Priya: That's helpful. I want to see the raw csv so we can evaluate with our eval harness.
[12:25] Jordan: We'll share the benchmark csv and an example Jupyter notebook to reproduce. We'll also include the config used (kernel selection, batch window, schd?).
[12:40] Mike: Another concern: network jitter between our app servers and Dedicated nodes — how do you handle retries without duplicating tokens?

[12:53] Samira: We have idempotent request IDs and a token-offset mechanism. The runtime can resume generation given last acked token id. For high jitter links we recommend co-located edge proxies to reduce RTT.
[13:10] Priya: For on-prem air-gapped, how long does installation and validation typically take?

[13:20] Emily: For a standard Dedicated install in your VPC it's a few days for network setup, then a 1-2 week validation for perf/security. For fully air-gapped on-prem with HSM and offline key flows expect 4-8 weeks depending on approvals.
[13:40] Daniel: Can Redwood's runtime run inside our k8s cluster or do you deploy a managed agent?

[13:48] Emily: We have both options: containerized runtime for customer k8s (we provide helm charts) or a managed node pool where Redwood manages the infra. For air-gapped setups we bring a pre-approved bundle and scripts.
[14:05] Mike: Any gotchas on Kubernetes scheduling for GPU-heavy shard deployments?

[14:12] Samira: You need topology-aware scheduling — GPU affinity and NIC bandwidth are important. Also ensure your kubelet's eviction thresholds don't kill long-lived KV cache processes; we recommend reserved memory and cpu for the runtime DaemonSet.
[14:30] Priya: One more around evaluation: for our summarization set, what success criteria should we track in the pilot?

[14:38] Jordan: We typically define: 1) latency SLO (median and p95), 2) cost per 1k tokens, 3) quality metric (ROUGE/QA pass rate threshold vs baseline), 4) reliability (uptime and fallback frequency). We'll draft a pilot SLO doc.
[14:55] Samira: Also key is cache hit rate — it's a composite metric that explains a lot about cost and tail latency. We'll instrument that in the dashboard.
[15:10] Mike: Nice. On benchmarking methodology, please include both synthetic tail tests and replaying production traces — we want to see both.
[15:20] Samira: Agreed — we'll replay a sampled week of traffic and also run synthetic worst-case cold-cache scenarios.
[15:30] Priya: About cost optimization — does Redwood Optimize recommend quantization profiles automatically?
[15:37] Emily: Yes, Optimize can suggest profiles based on workload, target quality loss, and unit cost. It can propose Q4 with more GPUs vs int8 fewer GPUs tradeoffs and estimate cost/latency.
[15:50] Daniel: Let's call out the specific risk: model drift when quantizing finetuned models. Have you seen issues?

[15:58] Samira: Occasionally for some finetunes quantization changes token probability distributions; we do per-prompt/metric evals in the pipeline and will flag prompts that regress. That's part of the quality gating before rolling quantized variants to prod.
[16:20] Mike: For the pilot, can we start with a small Dedicated pool and scale up if cache hit rates suggest benefit?
[16:28] Jordan: Yep — we can do a canary: start with 4 GPUs in Dedicated, run the replay, examine hit rates, then expand to 8 or 16 as needed. Autoscaling policies can handle bursts.
[16:40] Priya: On metrics to watch during pilot: cache hit rate, prefetch latency, batching window distribution, p95/p99 token latency, and cost per request.
[16:50] Samira: Exactly. We'll give a dashboard with those charts and the raw csv for forensic analysis.
[17:05] Mike: Anything else on attention optimizations? We heard about sliding-window attention and mixed attention.

[17:12] Samira: We use a combination: local attention for very long contexts, global attention on important tokens, and attention caching. For models that support FlashAttention or fused kernels we turn those on; for extremely long sequences we sometimes use block-sparse approaches to get O(n * log n) behavior for some workloads.
[17:40] Priya: How do you handle alignment of tokenization across chunks so the model doesn't get confused mid-sentence?

[17:48] Emily: Our chunker aligns on semantic boundaries where possible, and we carry over last partial tokens between chunks. We also use overlap windows to avoid breaking tokens; the playback includes small overlaps to preserve coherence.
[17:58] Daniel: Are there any known model families that are particularly bad for 128k contexts?

[18:05] Samira: Some older architectures without KV cache or with very inefficient attention blow up in memory; transformers with well-implemented KV cache and attention fusion are best. Llama-3-like implementations with optimized kernels fare well, but always test your finetune.
[18:25] Mike: Cool. Let's recap next steps and owners.

[18:30] Jordan: Recap: Samira runs benchmarks on Atlas 8xA100 (and H100 if available) with your sample dataset and uploads csv; Emily shares VPC/on-prem checklist and KMS notes; Jordan sends SOW + pricing; OpenEnterprise provides sample dataset and redaction requirements. Schedule pilot kickoff week of Aug 17. Any objections?
[18:52] Priya: No objections. Sounds good.
[18:57] Aisha: Add security review session after we get the checklist.
[19:02] Jordan: Noted — we'll schedule a security deep-dive once Emily uploads docs.
[19:10] Mike: Thanks everyone. We'll review the csv and get back with dates for the pilot kickoff.
[19:18] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up with materials. End call.
